editorNote: Two very different machines reach the same buyer this spring, and the trade press finally puts them side by side.
morningLine: IBM's Peanut and Apple's Macintosh go head to head on the newsstand while Atari sells its arcade library to everybody else's hardware.

lead.headline: The Peanut Meets the Mac: IBM and Apple Fight for the Next Home Buyer
lead.dek: TIME's April 2 report frames two incompatible visions of personal computing, one betting on compatibility, the other on the mouse.
body: The comparison that dealers have been making informally since January reached the national press this week. In its April 2 technology report, TIME set IBM's PCjr against Apple's Macintosh and described the two as new entries battling for attention from the same undecided buyer. The deck put it plainly: new entries from IBM and Apple battle for attention.

IBM's approach is continuity. The PCjr is an 8088-class machine sold in 64K and 128K configurations, extending the DOS world downward into the family room with better color and sound than the office PC offers. The strategy assumes buyers want the thing their employer already uses, only cheaper. The execution has been the problem: the infrared chiclet keyboard drew ridicule from the first demonstrations, and the machine's compatibility with the PC software library is incomplete enough that dealers must check titles case by case.

Apple's approach is discontinuity. The Macintosh puts a Motorola 68000 behind a built-in nine-inch monochrome display, packs 128K of memory and a 400K three-and-a-half-inch floppy into a case a clerk can carry with one hand, and ships a mouse as standard equipment rather than an accessory. Windows, icons and pull-down menus are not options in the Macintosh; they are the only way in. The list price is $2,495.

The two machines therefore ask the buyer a question the industry has avoided since the Apple II: is a personal computer a smaller version of the office machine, or a different kind of appliance altogether? IBM's answer protects an installed base and a software catalog worth thousands of titles. Apple's answer discards both and asks the customer to trust that pointing at pictures beats typing commands.

Neither answer has been settled by sales. What the week established is that the trade has stopped treating the two as separate stories. For the rest of 1984, every home-computer purchase decision will be argued in these terms.

stories.headline: Atari Invades Rival Machines With a Dozen Atarisoft Games
body: Atari has released twelve of its games for competing computers and videogame consoles under a new software label, ATARISOFT, COMPUTE! reports in its April issue. The line puts arcade properties long identified with Atari hardware onto the Commodore 64, VIC-20, Apple II, IBM PC, ColecoVision and TI-99/4A, depending on the title.

The move is an admission with a price tag attached. Atari's console business has spent a year contracting, and the company's most durable asset is no longer its hardware but the names on its cartridge labels. Selling those names to owners of rival machines converts a shrinking hardware franchise into a software one.

For the shopper the effect is immediate and slightly disorienting: familiar Atari boxes now sit on the Commodore shelf. For the industry it marks something larger. Software rights and recognizable games are becoming separable from the manufacturer that first shipped them, and the cartridge is no longer a proof of loyalty to any one machine.

stories.headline: PC Boom Turns Into a Stock-Market Crapshoot
body: John Case's analysis for Inc., published April 1, looks past the product announcements at the investors funding them and finds a wreck. “If you're a stockholder in the personal computer business, you've probably had your head handed to you by now,” Peter Wright, vice president of Gartner Group Advisory Inc., told the magazine.

The piece treats personal-computer investing as a contest shaped by IBM's gravitational pull, price cuts that arrive faster than inventory turns, and genuine uncertainty about which vendors will still be shipping in two years. A crowded field of machines is not the same thing as a crowded field of survivors.

Read alongside the week's launch coverage, the analysis supplies the counterweight. The same spring that produces the PCjr, the Macintosh and the Mindset is producing a shakeout, and the two facts are not in tension. They are the same fact seen from the showroom and from the ticker.

stories.headline: Mindset Pushes PC Graphics Beyond the IBM Mold
body: BYTE's April issue lists the Mindset personal computer among its notable contents, and the machine deserves the attention for reasons that have nothing to do with spreadsheet compatibility. It runs MS-DOS on an Intel 80186, but it is not a conventional full clone of the IBM PC.

The difference is custom graphics hardware. The Mindset supports 320-by-200 graphics with sixteen simultaneous colors chosen from a 512-color palette, with hardware assistance for drawing and animation rather than the software-only redraw that slows other MS-DOS machines. Optional equipment allows work with NTSC video input and output, aiming the system at titling and graphics production.

Surviving service documentation dated April 1984 confirms the system was entering supported commercial use this spring. Whether the market rewards a graphics-minded MS-DOS machine is another question, and one the same week's business coverage suggests will be answered harshly.

stories.headline: Jobs Sells the Macintosh as a Mission, Not Just a Machine
body: Joseph P. Kahn's profile of Steven Jobs, published April 1 by Inc., catches Apple's chairman before an audience in Boston's John Hancock Hall running a tightly staged audiovisual presentation. The subject is a computer; the register is evangelical.

The profile supplies period texture the specification sheets cannot. Apple is not merely selling a 68000 and a mouse for $2,495. It is selling a claim about how ordinary people should meet a computer, and the pitch is delivered with the conviction of someone who expects to be proved right in public.
